name: Canthal tilt filter

lead: The canthal tilt filter is a TikTok camera effect that overlays a red line across a person's eyes and labels the tilt as positive, neutral or negative. Canthal tilt is the angle between the inner and outer corners of the eye.

Its appearance use is twofold. In looksmaxxing talk, an upward tilt is traditionally viewed as attractive and youthful, so people use the filter to check their own. Many other users instead followed the red line to draw a winged eyeliner flick that suits their eye shape.

paras: Users open the effect in the TikTok camera, hold the phone to their face so the line appears, and read the tilt label or draw eyeliner along the line. Videos of the check circulated widely in mid-2023.

There is no physical risk. Commentators including a clinical psychologist and an author on beauty standards have warned that rating features this way can encourage harsh self-judgment, and plastic surgeons quoted in coverage cautioned against permanent eye alterations.

chain: Filter marks the line through both eye corners
User sees their tilt label or the line's angle
Check the eye shape against the upward-tilt ideal, or follow the line with liner
A lifted-looking eye through makeup or further research into options
angle.text: The filter shows a person their eye angle, and many use the line as a template for an upward winged eyeliner. It is a visual guide rather than a treatment.

lead: The canthal tilt filter is a TikTok effect that draws a red line across the corners of the eyes to classify canthal tilt as positive (upward), neutral or negative (downward).[1] It spread in mid-2023, and HuffPost covered it on 23 August 2023.[1]

Surgeons quoted in the coverage said an upward tilt is traditionally seen as attractive and can contribute to a youthful look, while stressing that a negative tilt does not make someone unattractive.[1] Dexerto reported on 2 October 2023 that users had found the red line useful as a guide for winged eyeliner, drawing the wing along it to suit their eye shape.[2]
No studies have examined the filter itself.

paras: The effect places a red line across both eyes and labels the tilt.[1] Dexerto's guide describes opening the TikTok camera, searching Effects for Canthal Tilt, and aligning the line with the face.[2]

Plastic surgeons Anthony Youn, Ari Hoschander and Samuel Lin were quoted by HuffPost saying upward tilt is traditionally seen as attractive but is one of many facial factors and that trends change; Hoschander warned strongly against permanent eye alterations.[1] Journalist Elise Hu argued the trend sets an unreachable standard, and psychologist Ramani Durvasula said looksmaxxing-style pursuits can resemble body dysmorphia and harm young people.[1] Coverage noted that users with a negative tilt received negative comments.[1]
Others treated the filter mainly as a makeup tool, using the line to place eyeliner flicks.[2]

timeline.event: Filter spreads on TikTok; HuffPost coverage on 23 August.[1]
Dexerto publishes an eyeliner guide using the filter on 2 October.[2]
